candidate.blueprint_topic: Standard and Contact Precautions for fecal-oral infection risk
candidate.educational_objective: Apply CDC isolation guidance by using Contact plus Standard Precautions for a hospitalized patient with hepatitis A who is fecally incontinent, while reinforcing hand hygiene and fecal-contamination control because HAV is transmitted primarily by the fecal-oral route.

options.A: Use Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions, with meticulous hand hygiene and measures to prevent fecal contamination of the environment.
options.B: Use Standard Precautions only because hepatitis A never requires additional transmission-based precautions in adults.
options.C: Use Airborne Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily spread by inhalation of respiratory aerosols.
options.D: Use Droplet Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily transmitted by respiratory secretions during coughing and sneezing.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies hepatitis A as primarily transmitted by the fecal-oral route. In CDC Appendix A, viral hepatitis A generally requires Standard Precautions, but diapered or incontinent patients require Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions. CDC also notes that healthcare-associated hepatitis A transmission has been associated with fecal incontinence and inadequate hand hygiene, making meticulous hand hygiene and environmental contamination control directly relevant in this scenario. B is incorrect because fecal incontinence is the specific condition that changes the precaution requirement from Standard alone to Contact plus Standard. C and D are incorrect because hepatitis A is not primarily transmitted by airborne or respiratory-droplet routes. The final item deliberately includes fecal incontinence in the stem so that Contact Precautions are uniquely indicated rather than creating ambiguity with uncomplicated hepatitis A, for which Standard Precautions are generally sufficient.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports fecal-oral transmission of HAV, Standard Precautions for uncomplicated hepatitis A, Contact plus Standard Precautions for diapered or incontinent hepatitis A patients, and the importance of hand hygiene and control of fecal contamination in healthcare settings.
